Title: Protecting Digital Liberties: The Case for Unrestricted Virtual Expression

In the realm of virtual reality (VR), the line between reality and simulation blurs, raising questions about whether the law should govern actions within these digital environments. Opponents of free expression within VR argue that simulated illegal or harmful acts could spill over into real-world harm. However, this perspective misapplies legal principles and underestimates the human capacity to differentiate between virtual and physical reality. The simulation of harmful acts within VR constitutes protected free expression under the First Amendment and does not lead to tangible real-world harm. Banning such expression would set a dangerous precedent for censorship, stifling creativity and innovation while failing to address the root causes of societal harms.

I. Simulated Acts as Protected Speech

The First Amendment safeguards not only written and spoken words but also symbolic speech—actions that convey ideas or messages. Supreme Court rulings, such as Texas v. Johnson (1989), affirmed that burning a flag as protest is expressive and protected, even if offensive. Similarly, VR simulations represent a new medium of expression. Whether a user recreates a violent act or engages in role-play, these simulations communicate ideas, critique societal norms, or explore ethical boundaries. To restrict these virtual acts would be tantamount to banning a dystopian novel or graphic art, which are protected even if they depict morally questionable scenarios.

Jurisprudence on video games further supports this view. In Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association (2011), the Supreme Court ruled that depictions of violence in games are entitled to free speech protections, rejecting claims that such content incites violence. VR, as an immersive extension of video games, should receive equal treatment. Just as films and books are not regulated for displaying dangerous acts, VR’s simulated actions are mere representations and thus fall under the umbrella of artistic and creative expression.

II. Absence of Tangible Harm Warrants Legal Toleration

Critics argue that simulated violence could desensitize individuals or normalize harmful behavior. However, decades of research on media violence have failed to establish a causal link between virtual violence and real-world aggression. Studies, such as the American Psychological Association’s 2015 review, found no conclusive evidence that VR or video games cause aggressive behavior. Human psychology demonstrates that participants in VR understand their actions lack real-world consequences—they don’t physically hurt another human or property. The harm must be real, not hypothetical, to warrant restriction.

Moreover, the absence of physical harm removes the threat of tangible injury. Unlike incitement to violence, which the First Amendment permits to be restricted under Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969), simulated acts pose no imminent threat. A virtual murder or robbery lacks the capacity to incite a crowd because the simulation occurs in an isolated digital space. Users engage knowing their actions are intangible; no one is actually harmed, and the law has no legitimate interest in policing imagination or symbolic acts unless they directly produce harm.

III. Overreach Threatens Innovation and Autonomy

Restricting VR’s content risks a chilling effect on artistic creativity and technological progress. VR’s potential for education—such as simulating historical events or medical training—is compromised if creators self-censor to avoid legal scrutiny. Worse, regulating virtual acts sets a precarious precedent for state control over immersive experiences. If governments can dictate what users can simulate, they may extend this authority to curtail other forms of legal, expressive conduct. As Justice Black famously argued, “The Bill of Rights is not the law of the land—it’s the law of the people’s rights.”

Furthermore, the virtual space offers a safe arena to explore taboo subjects, fostering empathy and understanding. A person virtually confronting systemic oppression might develop compassion, just as literature or theater has done. To criminalize such exploration would stifle societal growth and moral inquiry.

IV. Counterarguments and Rebuttals

Some contend that VR could be used maliciously—for instance, allowing users to rehearse real crimes. Yet these concerns conflate intent and simulation. A virtual simulation, by definition, involves no real-world preparation. The law already punishes planning and preparation for crimes in the real world; restricting simulations would target thought instead of action.

Others argue that minors might be unduly influenced. However, safeguards such as age restrictions or parental controls can address this without outright bans. Conclusion

VR is not a shadow reality but an expressive medium—a digital canvas for humanity to explore, critique, and understand complex human behaviors. The First Amendment exists to protect unpopular, controversial, and even controversial speech, not just the harmless or agreeable. To permit the unrestricted expression of virtual acts honors both the spirit of free expression and the imperative that governments refrain from policing imagination unless physical harm occurs. Regulating VR’s content would erode constitutional principles, hinder innovation, and reflect a misunderstanding of how virtual worlds enrich human discourse. Just as Shakespeare’s Coriolanus depicts betrayal, or films like Sicario expose corruption, VR’s simulations deserve the same protections. Let us champion free expression in all its forms, even when it challenges our sensibilities, ensuring the Fourth Estate of the digital age remains free.

In a world where technology blurs reality, the law must remain tethered to foundational principles. To restrict virtual freedom today risks surrendering principles of liberty tomorrow. We stand on the precipice of a new creative frontier; we must ensure it grows under sunlight, not shadow.

Virtual Acts, Real Rights: The Case for Maximum Freedom of Expression in Virtual Reality

Virtual reality is rapidly becoming one of the most powerful artistic and expressive mediums ever created. Unlike books, films, paintings, or video games, VR can place people inside imagined worlds and allow them to participate in stories, fantasies, conflicts, and moral experiments with an unprecedented sense of presence. That power understandably unsettles some observers. When people encounter simulations of violence, crime, cruelty, or other disturbing conduct in VR, they may assume that the experience is morally equivalent to performing the same act in reality.

It is not.

A simulated act is not the act it depicts. A virtual theft does not deprive anyone of property. A virtual assault does not injure a body. A virtual murder does not end a life. The distinction between representation and reality is the foundation of free expression. If societies abandon that distinction merely because a new medium feels immersive, they risk treating thought, fantasy, art, and play as though they were physical crimes. That would be a profound threat to liberty.

The strongest default principle for virtual worlds should therefore be this: adults should be free to create, access, and participate in fictional simulations of illegal or harmful acts, provided that no real person is being directly harmed, exploited, coerced, stalked, defrauded, or subjected to nonconsensual use of their likeness or personal data. Virtual conduct involving fictional characters and consensual users should be protected as expression, not punished as real-world wrongdoing.

Simulation Is Not Reality

The central argument for virtual freedom is simple: moral and legal judgment must be based on real-world consequences, not on the mere appearance of wrongdoing.

Human beings have long used fiction to explore acts they would never endorse in real life. Literature contains murder, betrayal, war, revenge, torture, theft, and cruelty. Theater portrays crimes and atrocities. Films allow audiences to inhabit the perspectives of criminals, soldiers, monsters, and antiheroes. Games have long let players engage in simulated combat, destruction, and lawbreaking. Yet no serious legal system treats the reader of a murder mystery as a murderer, the actor playing a villain as a criminal, or the player of a crime game as guilty of theft.

VR does not erase this distinction. It makes fictional experience more vivid, but vividness is not criminality.

A person who role-plays a bank robbery in a virtual environment has not robbed a bank. No employee has been threatened, no customer has been terrified, no money has been taken, and no physical institution has been harmed. A person who participates in a violent fictional scenario has not physically attacked another person merely because the simulation contains an avatar, animation, or programmed response. The virtual world may represent harm, but representation is not the same as infliction.

If law and public policy begin treating virtual depictions as equivalent to real acts, then the principle has no clear stopping point. Would acting in a VR war simulation become equivalent to participating in war? Would fictional political violence become a criminal threat? Would a virtual prison escape be treated as evidence of criminal intent? Such reasoning would confuse imagination with conduct and reduce civil liberties to whatever level of comfort the public happens to feel toward a particular medium.

Free Expression Includes Unpleasant Expression

Free expression is meaningful only when it protects material that some people dislike, fear, or condemn. Pleasant, conventional, morally reassuring speech does not need much protection. The true test of a free society is whether it permits people to explore controversial, disturbing, or unpopular ideas without treating them as criminals.

Virtual reality is not merely entertainment. It can be art, theater, political satire, historical reenactment, social criticism, psychological exploration, education, escapism, and personal fantasy. A VR creator may make a simulation of crime to criticize economic inequality, examine corruption, tell a story about survival, or explore the moral consequences of violence. Another person may use a disturbing fictional scenario to confront fears in a controlled environment. Someone else may simply enjoy a fantastical, unrealistic experience with no real-world meaning beyond play.

Governments and institutions should not appoint themselves as universal judges of which fantasies are acceptable. History repeatedly shows that censorship expands when authorities are granted broad power to suppress material deemed immoral, offensive, dangerous, or psychologically unhealthy. What begins with restrictions on obvious fictional violence can become restrictions on political dissent, unconventional sexuality, religious criticism, controversial art, or minority viewpoints.

The answer to offensive expression is criticism, parental guidance, content labeling, voluntary filters, and personal choice—not blanket prohibition.

Adults Have a Right to Explore Fictional Worlds

A free society should recognize that adults possess moral agency. They are capable of distinguishing reality from fiction, choosing what experiences they want, and declining experiences they find upsetting. Not every person will want to participate in a violent or criminal simulation. Many people will find such content repugnant. Their right to avoid it should be respected.

But the right to avoid expression is not the right to ban it for everyone else.

VR platforms can provide content ratings, age gates, opt-in systems, warnings, accessibility settings, and tools that allow users to avoid particular themes. Communities can establish their own rules. Private platforms may choose to host only certain kinds of content. Families can make decisions for children. None of these measures require the state to criminalize fictional conduct or declare that virtual simulations are inherently equivalent to real-world harm.

The key principle is consent. Adults who knowingly enter a fictional environment should be free to participate in imaginative experiences that do not impose themselves on unwilling people. Someone who dislikes a particular virtual scenario should not be forced into it; equally, someone who wishes to engage with legal fictional content should not be treated as dangerous merely for doing so.

Fear of “Desensitization” Is Not a Basis for Censorship

Opponents of virtual freedom often argue that immersive simulations may desensitize people to violence or encourage real-world wrongdoing. Such concerns may be worth studying, but they do not justify treating fictional activity as inherently criminal or harmful.

People have made similar claims about novels, comic books, rock music, films, television, role-playing games, and conventional video games. Again and again, cultural anxieties have predicted moral collapse from fictional entertainment. Again and again, those predictions have proven exaggerated or unsupported.

More importantly, even if particular media experiences affect some individuals differently, that does not establish a general justification for censorship. Many forms of expression can influence emotions, attitudes, and behavior. Political speeches can inspire anger. Religious messages can motivate sacrifice. News coverage can create fear. Fiction can evoke sympathy, disgust, sadness, or excitement. A democracy cannot preserve freedom by banning every form of expression that might affect someone psychologically.

The appropriate response to uncertain concerns is research, education, optional safeguards, and support for people who need it—not the criminalization of imagination.

The Necessary Boundary: Real-World Victims and Nonconsensual Conduct

Defending broad freedom for fictional VR does not require denying that some conduct associated with VR can cause real harm. The distinction is straightforward: law should address real-world victims, coercion, exploitation, fraud, harassment, privacy violations, and the use of real people without consent—not fictional scenarios involving consenting participants and invented characters.

For example, it is reasonable to prohibit:

  • Nonconsensual use of a real person’s likeness, voice, biometric data, or private information.
  • Targeted harassment of real users within a VR platform.
  • Credible threats directed at identifiable real people.
  • Fraud, blackmail, stalking, or coercion conducted through VR systems.
  • Exploitation of minors or any situation involving actual abuse or coercion.
  • Distribution of personal data or recordings without consent.

These restrictions do not undermine expressive freedom. They protect people from concrete, identifiable harm. The law should intervene when virtual technology becomes a tool for violating the rights of actual human beings—not merely because a fictional world depicts conduct that would be illegal outside it.

This distinction is essential. A free society can oppose real exploitation while defending fictional expression. It can protect people from harassment while refusing to criminalize imagination. It can punish conduct that creates victims without turning every disturbing fantasy into evidence of moral guilt.

Virtual Freedom Can Strengthen, Not Weaken, Society

Allowing people to explore difficult material in fictional settings may serve useful social purposes. Virtual environments can help creators depict the brutality of war, the consequences of oppression, the fear of victimization, or the moral complexity of crime. They can allow users to experience stories from perspectives radically different from their own. They can create controlled spaces for dramatic role-play, artistic experimentation, and emotional exploration.

A society that bans all simulated wrongdoing would not become more moral; it would become less capable of representing moral conflict honestly. Great art often examines humanity at its worst in order to reveal something important about humanity at its best. Fictional depictions of wrongdoing can produce empathy, reflection, criticism, and understanding. They can also simply entertain. Neither purpose should require permission from censors.

The desire to regulate virtual worlds often rests on the belief that people cannot be trusted with their own minds. But freedom requires trust in individual judgment. It requires accepting that adults may think dark thoughts, consume uncomfortable art, and participate in fictional scenarios without becoming criminals. The law should punish real violence, not imagined violence; real theft, not simulated theft; real coercion, not consensual role-play.

Conclusion

Virtual reality should be governed by the same fundamental principle that protects books, films, theater, games, and other forms of fiction: depiction is not commission, imagination is not intent, and simulation is not reality.

The most defensible approach is maximum protection for fictional, consensual virtual expression, paired with firm legal protections against actual harms such as harassment, exploitation, privacy violations, fraud, coercion, and nonconsensual use of real people’s identities. Within those boundaries, adults should be free to explore even disturbing fictional material without being treated as though they have committed real crimes.

A society confident in freedom does not fear every dark story, every uncomfortable fantasy, or every simulated act. It recognizes that liberty includes the freedom to imagine what one would never do, to portray what one condemns, and to enter fictional worlds without surrendering one’s real-world rights.

Yet, when an individual in VR “commits a murder,” “steals a car,” or “destroys a building,” no blood is spilled, no property is lost, no trauma is inflicted—except, perhaps, to the participant’s own sense of guilt or catharsis, which remains a private, internal experience. One of the most compelling arguments in favor of broad protection for virtual conduct is that virtual reality, like literature, film, theater, and video games, is a medium of expression. This distinction is essential. A simulation involving entirely fictional, non-sentient characters raises different concerns from an environment where actual users are stalked, degraded, terrorized, or coerced through avatars. Even if no physical contact occurs, real people can suffer psychological distress, intimidation, or trauma from immersive abuse. Thus, the claim that virtual conduct causes “no real-world harm” cannot be universally maintained. Sometimes it may be true; sometimes it plainly is not.

In addition, fully unrestricted virtual environments may create difficult evidentiary and policy problems. Certain simulations could be used to rehearse criminal behavior, glorify exploitation, or facilitate extremist communities organized around abuse. It is not necessary to claim that every virtual depiction directly causes real-world violence in order to admit that some forms of immersive simulation may contribute to harmful norms or to the grooming, intimidation, or targeting of vulnerable users. The social impact may be indirect, but indirect harms can still matter.

Ethical Concerns Beyond Physical Injury

Even where no direct victim is present, ethical concerns remain. Societies do not evaluate conduct solely by whether it causes immediate bodily harm. They also consider dignity, consent, exploitation, and social meaning. A fully unrestricted regime would imply that all simulated abuse is beyond moral and legal concern so long as it remains virtual. But many people reject that conclusion because representations can shape attitudes and because some simulations may express degradation in ways that are culturally corrosive.

For example, there is a difference between depicting a crime in a narrative designed to criticize it and constructing an immersive environment that invites users to celebrate domination or humiliation. Both may be expressive, but not all expression is socially equivalent. Freedom of expression is a legal principle, not a guarantee that every exercise of expression is ethically harmless. A mature society can defend civil liberties while still acknowledging that some forms of expression may normalize cruelty, commodify abuse, or undermine respect for others.

Moreover, in commercial VR platforms, companies have responsibilities not only to abstract liberty but also to user safety. Communities function only when participants believe they can enter shared spaces without being subjected to extreme harassment or simulated victimization. If “anything goes” becomes the rule, many users—especially children, marginalized groups, and trauma survivors—may be driven out. An unrestricted model can therefore reduce others’ freedom to participate.

The Best Path: Strong Protection With Real Limits

A more defensible position is that virtual reality deserves robust free-expression protection, but not absolute immunity from regulation. The law should begin with a presumption in favor of expressive freedom, especially for fictional, private, single-user simulations that do not involve real victims, non-consensual interaction, or criminal coordination. Adults should generally be free to engage with disturbing fictional content, and governments should be wary of censorship based only on moral disapproval.

At the same time, clear limits are justified where virtual conduct crosses into targeted harassment, non-consensual interaction, exploitation of real persons, credible threats, criminal planning, or material that is unlawful for reasons extending beyond its expressive content. Multiplayer VR platforms should be allowed—and in many cases expected—to create rules against immersive abuse. Age restrictions, transparency tools, moderation systems, consent-based boundaries, and user-controlled safety settings can preserve freedom while reducing preventable harm.

This framework avoids two extremes. It rejects the claim that all simulated acts are equivalent to real crimes and therefore should be broadly banned. But it also rejects the simplistic view that virtual actions are always harmless merely because they are not physically real. The truth is more complex: some virtual experiences are best understood as protected fiction, while others can function as real harassment or contribute to real harm.

Virtual reality forces society to rethink old categories of speech, conduct, fantasy, and harm. There is strong reason to protect immersive simulation as a form of free expression, especially when it involves fictional content and consenting adults. Democracies should be reluctant to criminalize imagined acts simply because they are offensive or disturbing. However, the claim that all simulated harmful conduct causes no real-world harm is too sweeping to be sustained. VR can affect real people in real ways, particularly in shared interactive environments. The most persuasive and principled position is therefore one of broad but not unlimited freedom: protect virtual expression vigorously, but recognize meaningful limits where consent, safety, and tangible human impact are at stake.

The Case for Unrestricted Virtual Harm: Free Expression in Simulated Reality

Introduction

In an era where virtual reality (VR) and digital simulation are becoming increasingly sophisticated, the boundaries between the real and the virtual are blurring. While some argue that simulating illegal or harmful acts in virtual environments is morally reprehensible, others contend that such activities are a fundamental extension of free expression—one that, when properly contained, poses no real-world consequences. Free Expression as a Fundamental Right

The most compelling argument for unrestricted virtual simulation of illegal or harmful acts rests on the principle of free expression. The First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, and similar protections in other democratic societies, guarantee the right to speak, write, and act without government interference—so long as the expression does not incite violence or harm in a tangible, real-world sense.

In the digital realm, this principle extends naturally. Just as a person can freely write a novel depicting a murder or a play where a character commits a crime, they should be able to engage in a virtual environment where such actions occur without legal repercussions. The difference between a written or filmed depiction and a fully immersive VR experience is one of medium, not morality. If a book or film depicting a crime is protected under free expression, then why should a VR simulation be any less so?

Moreover, virtual reality allows for nuanced, interactive experiences that traditional media cannot replicate. A player can step into a virtual world where they are the perpetrator of a crime, experiencing the consequences firsthand—without ever leaving their home. This is not just entertainment; it is a form of artistic and educational expression that challenges societal norms in ways that are impossible in the physical world.

The Distinction Between Virtual and Real-World Harm

A common counterargument to unrestricted virtual simulation is that such activities could lead to real-world harm. However, this claim is flawed because virtual experiences are inherently non-physical. Unlike physical actions, VR simulations do not cause tangible damage to people, property, or ecosystems. A person cannot be physically harmed by a virtual murder, nor can a virtual crime leave a permanent mark on the real world.

Some may argue that psychological harm could occur, but even this is debatable. While intense VR experiences might evoke strong emotions, they do not result in real-world violence, addiction, or lasting trauma in the same way that physical harm does. Studies on VR and its psychological effects are still emerging, but there is no evidence that unrestricted virtual simulations lead to real-world criminal behavior. In fact, many argue that such simulations could be used for therapeutic purposes—helping individuals confront and process difficult experiences in a controlled environment.

Furthermore, the risk of real-world harm is mitigated by the fact that VR environments are self-contained. Unlike online gaming or social media, where users might interact with others in ways that could escalate into real-world conflict, VR simulations are typically solitary experiences. The only potential for harm would be if someone were to attempt to replicate a virtual crime in the real world—but this is no different from someone reading a novel about a murder and deciding to commit one themselves. The difference is that the novel does not cause harm in the same way.

The Educational and Psychological Benefits

Beyond free expression, unrestricted virtual simulations could serve significant educational and psychological purposes. Many people struggle with moral dilemmas, ethical decision-making, or difficult historical events. A VR experience where a user can witness a crime unfold and then choose how to respond—without real-world consequences—could be an invaluable tool for education and personal growth.

For example, a VR simulation of a historical massacre could help students understand the human cost of war without the emotional trauma of real-life exposure. Similarly, a virtual prison experience could teach empathy and the consequences of criminal behavior in a safe, controlled setting. These simulations could also be used in therapy, helping individuals process trauma or phobias by exposing them to dangerous or taboo scenarios in a virtual space where they cannot cause harm.

The potential for psychological and educational benefits far outweighs any hypothetical risks of real-world harm. If we allow certain forms of free expression—such as depictions of violence in film or literature—then virtual simulations should follow the same principle.

The Evolution of Digital Expression

The digital world is constantly evolving, and with it, the boundaries of acceptable expression. In the past, a person could write a novel about a crime, but they could not experience it firsthand. Today, VR allows for full immersion—where a user can step into a virtual world and engage in actions that would otherwise be illegal.

In Defense of Radical Freedom in Virtual Reality: Why Simulated Acts Should Be Treated as Protected Expression

  1. VR as the next evolution of expressive media

The core democratic insight behind robust free-expression protections is that the state must not become an arbiter of acceptable imagination. History is replete with once-condemned art and media—violent plays, shocking novels, transgressive films, controversial games—initially blamed for corrupting youth or eroding morality.   • Fictional violence does not reliably translate into violent crime.
  • Disturbing art often functions as catharsis, critique, or exploration, not endorsement.

  • Filming a movie with actors portraying crimes.

The consistent principle must be: if no non-consenting, real-world person is directly harmed or exploited, the “act” is expressive and internal to the medium, not a crime. It is content—morally debatable, but politically protected.

To suddenly criminalize or broadly restrict virtual conduct because it feels intense would break with decades of jurisprudence and cultural practice that distinguish between representation and reality. A central moral and legal boundary is consent. Real harm arises when people are coerced, deceived, or placed into abusive situations against their will. But a purely virtual scenario, entered voluntarily by adults who understand its fictional nature, is different. In such a case:

  • Every participant is opting into an experience.
  • No one’s body is touched without consent.
  • No one’s property is actually destroyed.
